trails.trailTip: The trail's upper section connects to paved Hot Springs Mountain Drive near the observation tower, so budget extra time (and a small admission fee) if you want to ride the elevator up for panoramic Ouachita views.
trails.didYouKnow: The Hot Springs Mountain Tower sits atop the highest point in the park and has offered panoramic views of the Ouachita Mountains since 1983.

trails.trailTip: This point-to-point route is usually split into three shorter sections (West Mountain, Sugarloaf Mountain, and Stonebridge Road) and is closed to mountain bikes, so plan a car shuttle or hike a single segment as an out-and-back.
trails.didYouKnow: At over 10 miles one-way, the Sunset Trail is the longest continuous trail in the smallest national park in the system.

trails.trailTip: Starting right at Gulpha Gorge Campground makes this an easy add-on hike for campers; footing can get slick near creek crossings after rain.
trails.didYouKnow: Gulpha Gorge Campground sits atop the same geothermal aquifer that feeds the park's famous hot springs.

trails.trailTip: Visit in spring to catch the trail's namesake dogwood blooms lighting up the hardwood understory.
trails.didYouKnow: Hot Springs National Park's forest lies in the Ouachita Mountains, one of the few major east-west mountain ranges in North America.

trails.trailTip: Peak Trail is the most direct route from downtown Bathhouse Row to the mountaintop, making it easy to combine with a stroll along the historic row.
trails.didYouKnow: You can walk directly from a historic bathhouse to a mountain summit trailhead in Hot Springs — a rarity among national parks.

trails.trailTip: This short loop near Bathhouse Row is a good option when you only have an hour but still want a forested overlook of downtown.
trails.didYouKnow: North Mountain's overlooks give one of the best views of the historic Bathhouse Row streetscape below.

trails.trailTip: Goat Rock functions mainly as a connector between other park trails, so check a trail map before starting to plan your full route.
trails.didYouKnow: Many of Hot Springs' trails, including this one, were built or improved by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s.

trails.trailTip: A good pick for a quick wildflower walk below Hot Springs Mountain without committing to a full summit hike.
trails.didYouKnow: Hot Springs National Park protects thermal water estimated to have fallen as rain roughly 4,000 years ago before slowly percolating back to the surface.

animals.whereToLook: Forest edges along Gulpha Gorge and West Mountain trails
animals.viewingTip: Watch quietly from a distance with binoculars, especially near dawn, and give any doe with fawns a wide berth rather than approaching for a closer look.
animals.didYouKnow: White-tailed deer raise the white fur on the underside of their tail as a flash warning when alarmed, which is how they got their name.

animals.whereToLook: Wooded slopes and trail edges throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: Listen for gobbling at first light in spring and observe from the trail with binoculars rather than following a flock off-path.
animals.didYouKnow: Wild turkeys can run up to 25 mph and are strong short-distance fliers despite their size.

animals.whereToLook: Leaf litter along shaded sections of the Dogwood and Gulpha Gorge trails
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy a sighting from where you stand — box turtles can live 50+ years, and picking one up to move or 'help' it (unless it's in the road) does more harm than good.
animals.didYouKnow: A box turtle's hinged plastron lets it close its shell almost completely, one of the only turtles in North America able to do so.

animals.whereToLook: Mature forest along the North Mountain and Sunset trails
animals.viewingTip: Listen for its 'who-cooks-for-you' call at dusk and rely on your ears or a red-filtered flashlight — resist playing owl calls or recordings to lure it closer.
animals.didYouKnow: The barred owl's classic call is often phonetically remembered as 'Who cooks for you, who cooks for you all?'

animals.whereToLook: Leaf litter and rocky sections of forested trails
animals.viewingTip: Give copperheads several feet of space and watch where you step on leaf-covered trail sections — they rely on camouflage rather than fleeing, so never reach toward or attempt to move one.
animals.didYouKnow: A copperhead's banded pattern resembles a stack of Hershey's Kisses, which helps it disappear against dry leaves.

animals.viewingTip: Gray foxes are shy and rarely seen in daylight; a quiet dusk walk with binoculars is a better bet than trying to approach a den area.
animals.didYouKnow: The gray fox is one of the few canids that can climb trees, using curved claws to escape predators or reach fruit.

animals.whereToLook: Sunny rocks and logs along the Hot Springs Mountain and West Mountain trails
animals.viewingTip: Approach slowly and observe from a few feet away with the naked eye or binoculars — sudden movement will send it darting for cover.
animals.didYouKnow: Males do 'push-up' displays to show off the blue patches on their throat and belly to rivals and potential mates.

animals.whereToLook: Surrounding hills, occasionally heard from park trails
animals.viewingTip: You're far more likely to hear a coyote's yips and howls at night than to see one — enjoy the chorus from camp and never leave out food that could habituate them to people.
animals.didYouKnow: A coyote's nighttime chorus can sound like a much larger group than it really is because of how its yips echo through the hills.
